messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was fifty-seven when he came to his first appointment, though his face carried the weathered look of someone who had spent the last three years holding himself very still. He worked as a tutor, primarily with high school students in reading comprehension and writing, a profession he had chosen precisely because it allowed him to control the environment—he scheduled sessions in the public library, always at the same table in the corner, always with an exit in his line of sight. This had worked until recently, when the library underwent renovations and his usual spot was cordoned off. For two weeks he had sat at different tables, each one leaving him with a low, persistent dread that tightened his chest. He had finally stopped taking new students rather than face the uncertainty of where he would sit.

Three years earlier, Marcus had been assaulted by a man he had trusted—a colleague from a volunteer mentorship program. They had been alone in the man's apartment, ostensibly to discuss curriculum materials. What happened next existed in Marcus's mind as a series of vivid, unbearable fragments: the moment the man's hand had gripped his shoulder and he realized he could not move; the voice saying "don't fight me"; the absolute loss of what he had always believed was his to control. Marcus remembered the texture of the fabric against his skin, the weight of another person's body, the way his own body had betrayed him by freezing. But there were also gaps—stretches of time he could not account for, sensations he knew had occurred but could not quite locate in the sequence, words that had been said that he knew were important but could not quite form into language even now.

In the months after the assault, Marcus had begun to notice that he could not tolerate being touched. His sister had hugged him at a family dinner and he had flinched so violently that she had stepped back, hurt. He had stopped shaking hands with students' parents. He had not had a romantic relationship since. More than that, he had become someone who watched. At the grocery store, he tracked the movements of men around him—how they stood, whether they made eye contact, whether they seemed to be moving toward him or away. He chose his seat in restaurants based on which table allowed him to see the entrance and positioned his back against the wall. When he was in his apartment alone, he locked the door and checked it twice. When he was anywhere unfamiliar, he felt a creeping panic that made it impossible to concentrate, because he could not map the danger. He did not know where the exits were. He did not know who was behind him.

The thought that had come to dominate his waking hours was that his own body could no longer be trusted. It had not protected him. It had responded in ways he had not chosen. He had come to believe that vigilance was the only thing that stood between him and another catastrophe. He had to watch constantly. He had to control what he could control—where he sat, who he allowed near him, which situations he entered. This meant avoiding most things that carried emotional weight. He had stopped attending his church. He had declined his sister's invitation to his nephew's wedding. He had not been to a movie theater in three years. Instead, he had taken up smoking, something he had quit twenty years prior. The cigarettes gave him something to do with his hands when he felt the panic rising, and the act of smoking—the ritual, the control, the way it gave him a reason to be alone—had become a necessary part of his day.

What had finally brought him in was a student's parent, a man, who had asked to meet with Marcus to discuss his son's progress. Marcus had felt the familiar ice in his stomach at the prospect of being alone with this man in any space, even a public one. He had made an excuse. Then another. The parent had complained to the tutoring agency. Marcus had lost the client. Sitting in his apartment that evening, smoking and unable to sleep, he had realized that the assault was no longer something that had happened to him three years ago. It had become the thing that was happening to him every single day, in every moment he was not alone, in every choice about where to sit and who to trust and whether his own body would betray him again. He had called the clinic the next morning, though he still did not know if he believed that anything could actually change.
